The Strength of Israel
thuh STRENGKTH uv IZ-ray-el
n. phr. (a divine title, spoken by Samuel to Saul concerning God's unchangeableness)
Hebrew netsach Yisrael — netsach, which the AV margin itself glosses “or, Eternity, or, Victory”; the root carries endurance, perpetuity and the pre-eminence of one who outlasts and overcomes, so the title names God as Israel's unfailing permanence.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Saul has spared Agag and the best of the spoil, offered sacrifice as his excuse, and been told that to obey is better than sacrifice. When he clutches at Samuel's mantle and tears it, Samuel gives him the reason the kingdom will not be restored: “And also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent.” The title is rare and weighty. The Hebrew word is netsach, which the translators' own margin glosses as Eternity and as Victory, and either reading serves: God is Israel's permanence and Israel's triumph, the one who does not fail or change. The context is what makes the title a judgment. Saul wants the sentence reconsidered, and the answer is that the One who passed it is not a man that He should change His mind. The same chapter says two verses earlier that it repented the LORD that He had set up Saul, which teaches the reader how such language works: Scripture speaks of God relenting in the language of His dealings with men, and in the same breath denies that He is mutable in His nature or His purpose. The Reformed doctrine of divine immutability stands exactly here, and so does the sinner's only ground of hope, since an unchangeable God is as unchangeable in His promises as in His threatenings.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Strength, that property of a body by which it sustains the application of force without breaking; firmness; power. Israel, the covenant name given to Jacob and to the nation from him. The Strength of Israel, 1 Samuel 15:29, a divine title naming God's unchangeableness.

Strength, that property by which a body sustains force without breaking; firmness.

Israel, the name given to Jacob and to the nation descended from him.

Hebrew netsach, perpetuity, endurance; the AV margin adds ‘Eternity’ and ‘Victory’.

Hebrew shaqar, to lie or deal falsely — denied of Him in the same verse.

Hebrew nacham, to repent or relent — ‘he is not a man, that he should repent’.

Key Scripture

1Sa 15:29 — "And also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent."

Num 23:19 — "God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?"

Mal 3:6 — "For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed."

Jas 1:17 — "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning."

Modern Corruption

Open theism and process theology deny the very attribute this title names, and the verse is also pressed flat in the other direction until God's relenting language in the same chapter is treated as a mere figure of nothing.

expand to see more

Open theism, in Pinnock, Boyd and Sanders, holds that God does not exhaustively know or settle the future and genuinely changes His mind as history unfolds; process theology goes further and denies immutability and omnipotence outright. Samuel's title answers both in seven words: the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent, for he is not a man, that he should repent. Balaam is made to say the same thing, Malachi grounds Israel's survival in “I am the LORD, I change not”, and James says every good gift comes from the Father with whom is no variableness nor shadow of turning. A God who deliberates like a man is not the God of Scripture, and no promise of His could be trusted further than His next revision.

A second failure belongs to careless defenders of the doctrine, who meet the chapter's own statement that it repented the LORD that He had set up Saul by emptying the words of all content. Scripture is doing something more careful. God's dealings with men genuinely change as men change — He threatens Nineveh and spares it on repentance — while His nature and eternal purpose do not move at all; the Westminster and Baptist confessions say He is immutable and yet most just and terrible in His judgments. The principle to recover is both halves. Immutability is not divine indifference, and the relenting language is not divine instability; it is the unchangeable God dealing variously with changeable men.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew netsach, perpetuity or victory (the AV margin glosses both); with shaqar, to lie, and nacham, to relent — both denied of Him because He is not a man.
